name: Executive order of January 11, 1875 (addition to the Great Sioux Reservation east of the Missouri River)
nations: Lakota, Dakota and Nakota (Oceti Sakowin) of the Great Sioux Reservation
promises: The President withdrew from sale a large tract along the east bank of the Missouri River and set it apart 'for the use of the several tribes of Sioux Indians as an addition to their present reservation' (as quoted in 316 U.S. 317).
The reason given by the Commissioner of Indian Affairs and the Secretary of the Interior was the suppression of the liquor traffic with the Indians on the Missouri River (316 U.S. 317).
landTaken: Royce Area 614. Nearly all of it was restored to the public domain by executive order of August 9, 1879 and the remainder by executive order of March 20, 1884 (Royce schedule).
compensation: None. The Supreme Court held in 1942 that no compensation was owed (316 U.S. 317).
today: In Sioux Tribe of Indians v. United States, 316 U.S. 317 (decided 1942-05-11), the Sioux sued for some 5 1/2 million acres taken by the restoring orders of 1879 and 1884. The Supreme Court affirmed the Court of Claims in denying recovery, holding that these executive order additions gave the Sioux no compensable interest. That ruling went against the nation and is recorded here, not as a breach. The restorations are recorded under cession-1879-08-09-sioux and cession-1884-03-20-sioux.

openQuestions: The order's text was read through Royce's schedule and the Supreme Court's account of it; the UGA scan linked in treaties.json returned 403.
No tribal statement about the 1875 and 1876 additions east of the Missouri was found.
The Commissioner of Indian Affairs told settlers in 1875 that it was not 'supposed that the withdrawal will be made permanent' (316 U.S. 317); whether the Sioux were told the same was not found.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe's history says the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty fixed the Great Sioux Reservation's bounds and made no cession valid without three-fourths of the adult men, that an 1875 executive order moved Standing Rock's line north to the Cannon Ball River before Congress broke the reservation up in 1889, and that it holds its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights as binding today as when they were made.
